strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive, multi-faceted evaluation across 9 cybersecurity benchmarks, comparing against strong baselines (same-family instruct models), open-source cybersecurity-specialized models (DeepHat, Lily, Primus, Foundation-Sec), and closed frontier models (GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, Sec-Gemini v1), with consistently strong and often state-of-the-art results at a fraction of the parameter count.

The SecKnowledge 2.0 pipeline's expert-in-the-loop format generation system is a practical and well-motivated contribution to scaling domain-expert supervision across a large (105-task) label space, and is described with sufficient implementation detail (Appendix A.1, screenshots) to be conceptually reproducible.

Careful ablations isolate the contribution of the reformatting/enrichment pipeline versus the original SecKnowledge dataset and a standard ReAlign-style baseline, holding model size and training budget fixed, which provides reasonably convincing evidence that data-quality improvements (not just longer training or larger data) drive the gains.

The LLM-as-judge evaluation is validated against human expert preferences (>90% agreement with grounding), and quality-assessment metrics (readability, factuality) are reported per task with reasonable transparency (Fig. 9), improving confidence in the qualitative claims.

Useful practical findings for practitioners, e.g., base vs. post-trained model as fine-tuning starting point, quantization robustness (Appendix G), and prompt-loss masking observations, add value beyond the core method contribution.
weaknesses: No stated plan for releasing the SecKnowledge 2.0 dataset, model checkpoints, taxonomy classification code, or the format-generation tool, which significantly limits reproducibility of both the dataset and the reported results, especially given the dataset's centrality to the paper's claims.

Comparisons to true frontier closed models (Sec-Gemini v1, o1, GPT-4o) are restricted to only two benchmarks (CTIBench-MCQ/RCM) for cost reasons, so the headline claim of 'matching or surpassing frontier models' is only convincingly demonstrated on a narrow slice of the full evaluation suite; broader claims rest more heavily on comparisons to open-source baselines and same-family instruct models.

The data generation, task classification (for both SecKnowledge 2.0 enrichment and evaluation benchmark categorization), and LLM-as-judge quality assessment/preference evaluation all rely on LLM pipelines (gpt-oss-120B, o3) that were also used to construct or filter the training data itself, raising some risk of circularity or self-consistency bias in the reported quality/preference metrics that is not fully addressed.

The paper offers essentially no discussion of dual-use/ethical risk despite explicitly building models intended to reason over TTPs, exploits, attack paths, and detection evasion—a notable omission for a cybersecurity-capability paper, particularly given that the enrichment pipeline explicitly aims to produce more detailed, actionable technical content (as illustrated in Fig. 3's iframe/CAPEC example).

Statistical robustness is limited: no confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or significance testing are reported for benchmark score improvements, and the LLMaaJ pairwise study uses only 115 expert-authored questions, which is a fairly small open-ended evaluation set relative to the breadth of claims made.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior work (SecKnowledge, ReAlign/Fan et al. 2024)—the main technical contributions are a format-generation UI/workflow and a multi-step search-grounding recipe layered on existing techniques, which, while practically useful, represent more of an engineering/systems contribution than a fundamentally new method.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 9 core cybersecurity benchmarks, multiple model scales (4B-20B), comparisons against open-source cybersecurity models, general open-source model families, and closed frontier models (o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o, Sec-Gemini v1), plus real-world use cases (threat-report-to-TTP mapping, CVE reassessment, CyberSOCEval, secure code generation).

Well-designed ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each pipeline component (expert-written vs. generic formats, search/grounding, backbone LLM choice), providing good evidence that gains stem from the proposed methodology rather than confounds.

LLM-as-judge evaluation is validated against human cybersecurity experts (30 experts, 115 questions) with reported agreement rates, and bidirectional (position-swapped) comparisons are used to control for positional bias — a methodologically careful practice.

Practical deployment considerations are addressed in depth (quantization impact, inference latency across batch sizes/precisions, training time), which is valuable for an applied domain-specific SLM paper.

The expert-in-the-loop format-generation framework is a genuinely useful contribution for scaling schema-driven reformatting to large, hierarchical task taxonomies, and is described with sufficient implementation detail (Appendix A) to be reproducible.

Results are consistent and large in magnitude across model sizes (7-14% average gains, 16-31% gains on CTIBench-RCM), which is a meaningful practical contribution toward on-premise, cost-efficient cybersecurity LLMs.
weaknesses: Potential train/benchmark contamination risk: several evaluation benchmarks (Adversarial CTI, Weakness Impact Mapping, CTI Detection & Mitigation, CTI Relationship Prediction) were introduced by the same prior work (Levi et al., 2025) from which SecKnowledge (the base dataset for SecKnowledge 2.0) is derived. The paper does not explicitly discuss or verify that there is no overlap between the enrichment/training data and these evaluation sets, which undermines confidence in the reported gains on these specific benchmarks.

The core contribution is an incremental extension of prior work (SecKnowledge -> SecKnowledge 2.0, CyberPal.ai -> CyberPal 2.0); the main novelty (expert-in-the-loop format generation + retrieval-grounded reformatting) largely composes existing techniques (ReAlign-style reformatting, RAG) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods.

Comparison against genuine frontier models is restricted to only two benchmarks (CTIBench-MCQ/RCM) due to cost, limiting the generality of the claim that CyberPal 2.0 'matches or surpasses' frontier models across the full capability spectrum; performance on the broader 9-benchmark suite is only measured against same-family baselines and other open models, not against o1/Sec-Gemini v1/GPT-4o.

Minor numeric inconsistencies exist between the main table and appendix ablation table for the same model/benchmark (e.g., CyberPal-2.0-20B CTIBench-RCM appears as 87.40 in Table 1 but 84.7 in Table 11), raising a small concern about result reporting consistency.

Full reproducibility is limited: only the 20B model, pipeline code, and evaluation benchmarks are stated for release, while the actual SecKnowledge 2.0 dataset and the smaller model checkpoints (4B/8B/14B) release status is not clearly specified, and the underlying SecKnowledge seed corpus availability is unclear.

The quality-assessment methodology in the pipeline (LLMaaJ readability/factuality) uses the same class of models (gpt-oss backbone) that generated the data, creating a degree of self-referential evaluation that could inflate apparent data quality without fully independent verification.

The claimed scalability of the expert-in-the-loop system for 105 tasks is asserted but the actual human-hours/expert effort required is not quantified, making it hard to assess how practical this approach is for organizations without a dedicated security-expert team.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning nine cybersecurity benchmarks plus several real-world-inspired tasks (threat-report-to-TTP mapping, CVE reassessment, CyberSOCEval, secure-code generation), which is more thorough than most domain-LLM papers.

Careful ablation studies (Table 3, Appendix G) that isolate the contribution of expert-written formats vs. generic reformatting, search/grounding, and the choice of reformatting backbone LLM, lending some support to the causal claims about SecKnowledge 2.0.
Practical deployment-oriented analyses (quantization, inference latency, training time) that are useful for practitioners considering on-premises SLM deployment.
The expert-in-the-loop format-generation tool (Appendix A.1) is a reasonable engineering contribution that could ease future dataset curation for other specialized domains.
LLM-as-judge protocol is validated against human experts with reasonable agreement rates, adding some credibility to the qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The headline claim that the models 'match or surpass' frontier models (GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, Sec-Gemini v1) rests on only two benchmarks (CTIBench-MCQ/RCM); no frontier-model comparison is provided on the other seven benchmarks used elsewhere in the paper, so the strong abstract claims are not well supported by the breadth of evidence actually presented for that specific comparison.

Serious potential data-contamination/unfair-comparison risk: SecKnowledge/SecKnowledge 2.0 training data is synthesized directly from the same public taxonomies (CWE, CAPEC, ATT&CK, BRON) that underlie the CTI-RCM/MCQ and several other evaluation benchmarks. Fine-tuning directly on structured representations of these taxonomies and then evaluating recall/mapping over them is likely to inflate scores relative to general-purpose frontier models that were not specifically tuned on this exact taxonomy structure, undermining the fairness of the 'beats frontier models' narrative.

Results reported in the appendix undercut the paper's overall narrative of consistent improvement: on CyberSOCEval Threat Intelligence Reasoning (Table 14), CyberPal-2.0-8B actually scores lower in exact-match accuracy than its own Qwen3-8B baseline (38.61 vs 42.86), and on Secure Code Generation (Table 17) all CyberPal 2.0 variants show a consistent ~5-13 point drop versus their base/aligned counterparts. These are not minor details—they show the specialization pipeline can measurably degrade certain capabilities, yet this is downplayed and pushed to the appendix rather than integrated into the main narrative or abstract.

The core methodological novelty is incremental: it largely composes existing techniques (ReAlign-style reformatting, retrieval-augmented rewriting, LLM-as-judge filtering) with a bespoke expert-in-the-loop UI, rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling or data-generation principle.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs; all benchmark numbers appear to be single-run point estimates, which is a concern given some deltas (e.g., MCQ gains of 1-2 points against certain frontier baselines) are within plausible noise margins.

Evaluation protocol differences across compared models (thinking flag enabled for Qwen baselines vs. 'Medium' reasoning effort for gpt-oss, and unspecified settings for frontier closed models) raise questions about whether the head-to-head comparisons are fully controlled and reproducible by outside groups.

The expert-in-the-loop format design process, while assisted by an LLM, still requires substantial manual expert effort (105 tasks, iterative refinement) that is not clearly quantified in terms of person-hours, limiting practical reproducibility and scalability claims for other domains or task sets.

The impact/ethics statement is fairly generic; given the paper explicitly builds detailed TTP/attack-pattern/detection-evasion reasoning capability, more concrete detail on red-teaming methodology, misuse testing, or release safeguards would be warranted rather than a brief paragraph of intentions.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation: results span nine core cybersecurity benchmarks, comparisons to baselines, open-source cybersecurity models, other model families, and frontier closed models (Sec-Gemini v1, o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o), plus two additional real-world use-case evaluations (threat-report-to-TTP mapping and CVE reassessment) and further appendix evaluations (CyberSOCEval, secure code generation).

Thorough ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each pipeline component (expert-written formats vs. generic reformatting, backbone LLM choice, retrieval grounding), which convincingly attribute gains to the proposed pipeline rather than to reformatting alone.

Practical/deployment-oriented rigor: reports on quantization effects, inference latency across batch sizes and precisions, and training time, which is valuable for an SLM-focused contribution aimed at enterprise deployment.
LLM-as-a-judge protocol is validated against human expert agreement (80-90%), strengthening confidence in the pairwise preference results.
Reasonable transparency about data provenance, benchmark taxonomy construction, and an expert-in-the-loop system for defining task formats, with a documented UI and iterative refinement loop.

Strong reported gains (7-14% average) over same-family baselines and competitive/superior performance versus much larger frontier models on CTI-RCM/MCQ, which if verified would be a meaningful practical contribution.
weaknesses: Potential benchmark/training overlap risk: several evaluation benchmarks (Weakness Impact Mapping, Adversarial CTI, CTI Detect & Mitigate, CTI Relationship Prediction, CISSP Exams) are introduced by the same author group's prior work and may draw on similar underlying sources (CWE, MITRE, CAPEC, BRON) as the SecKnowledge training data; the paper does not clearly demonstrate absence of train/test leakage for these in-house benchmarks.

Frontier-model comparisons (Sec-Gemini v1, o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o) rely on reported/limited-cost evaluation restricted to only two benchmarks (CTIBench-MCQ/RCM) with numbers seemingly drawn from external reports rather than a fully controlled, identical evaluation harness across all systems, which limits the strength of the head-to-head claims.

Ablation studies (Table 3) are conducted only on the smallest 4B model; it is unclear whether the relative contributions of each pipeline component (formats, search, backbone LLM) generalize to the 8B/14B/20B models.

Only the 20B model and pipeline/benchmarks are stated for release; the smaller (and best cost-performance) variants are not clearly committed to open release, limiting full reproducibility of the model suite's headline results.

No variance/multiple-run reporting or statistical significance testing is provided for benchmark scores or ablations, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., single-point percentage differences) are robust to noise.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental—an application/extension of existing reformatting (ReAlign-style) and retrieval-grounding ideas with expert-in-the-loop format design—rather than a fundamentally new technique, though the engineering integration and empirical scale are non-trivial.

The CVE reassessment and threat-report-to-TTP benchmarks are relatively small-scale, single-annotator/limited-expert constructed evaluations, and details on inter-annotator agreement or dataset size are sparse, raising some concern about label noise and generalizability of the real-world use-case claims.

The impact statement's mitigation claims (red-teaming, responsible-use terms) are stated as future intentions rather than substantiated with actual red-teaming results or misuse-risk evaluation in the current submission.
